pages.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018

timeline.detail: Rann's county history records no building on the corner in 1825.
timeline.quote: as Rann indicates no structure was there in 1825.

timeline.what: Building shown on Ammi B. Young map
timeline.detail: The 1830 map shows a rectangular footprint similar to the present building.
timeline.quote: Our earliest map, the 1830 Ammi Burnham Young map, shows a similar rectangular footprint to the one currently occupied by the Leunig’s Building

timeline.detail: Hagar had been in business on the corner since 1836; 'Hagar & Arthur' advertised hardware, drugs and paints by 1848. I.M. Hagar later traded at 174 College St.
timeline.quote: Hagar had been in business there since 1836.

timeline.what: Present building constructed under shared-ownership contract
timeline.detail: Owners agreed to build one Federal-style structure shared between them; the split ownership explains the divided east facade. The page calls this the building that stands today, greatly altered.
timeline.quote: in 1847 the owners entered into an unusual contract where a new building would be constructed with both owners sharing ownership in this single structure.

timeline.what: Divided storefronts shown on Sanborn map
timeline.detail: The 1869 Sanborn map shows storefronts numbered 115 and 113 on Church St and a separate business at 174 College St.
timeline.quote: Our earliest Sanborn Fire Insurance map of 1869 reflects this as the original delineation of the building as the storefronts on Church Street, numbered 115 and 113, seem to follow the façade’s division.

timeline.what: Central Drug Store at 115 Church St
timeline.detail: Tobacco and drug store that opened June 1875 on the corner and lasted, under changing names and owners, until after a 1929 fire; it closed the following year after over fifty years.
timeline.quote: it was occupied by the Central Drug Store, which opened in June 1875, at the “corner of Church and College Sts”

timeline.what: Morris Abraham opens cigar store at 113 Church St
timeline.detail: Morris Abraham opened a cigar and tobacco store at 113 Church St, making cigars on the upper floors.
timeline.quote: before coming to Burlington to open up a store in 1889.

timeline.what: Abraham's Cut-Rate Drug Store; 'Patent Medicine War'
timeline.detail: Abraham added drugs in 1899, angering other druggists; the Burlington Free Press reported a 'Patent Medicine War'.
timeline.quote: in 1899, he bills his business as “Abraham’s Cut-Rate Drug Store.”

timeline.what: Bijou Tobacco Store at 115 Church St
timeline.detail: A competing tobacco store opened on the corner three months after the dispute.
timeline.quote: After the great “Patent Medicine War of 1899,” The Bijou Tobacco Store took up residence on this corner

timeline.detail: Morris's nephew Hyman Abraham came to Burlington after his uncle's death and was proprietor by the early 1920s.
timeline.quote: by the early 1920s he was the proprietor.

timeline.what: Hagar Hardware leaves for 98 Church St
timeline.detail: Hagar opened a second store at 98 Church St in the early 1920s and moved there entirely in 1923.
timeline.quote: In the early 1920’s Hagar Hardware and Paint Company opened up another story nearby at 98 Church Street before moving there entirely in 1923.

timeline.detail: A Christmas Eve 1929 fire caused about $20,000 in damage to the store's interior and stock.
timeline.quote: the Central Drug Store would endure here until Christmas Eve 1929, when a fire broke out, extensively damaging interior and stock of the business to the tune of $20,000.

timeline.what: W.E. Peters florist shop (174 College St section)
timeline.detail: A few years after Hagar left, W.E. Peters bought this section for his florist shop. In late 1932 the building was put up for forced sale and bought by the Chittenden County Trust Company. The page also gives Peters' new address as 128 Church.
timeline.quote: In late 1932, his brick building and all his business’s contents were put up for a forced sale

timeline.what: Hyman Abraham buys 174 College St section; Art Deco storefront
timeline.detail: The bank sold the space to Hyman Abraham in July 1933, starting his real estate business. Architect Louis S. Newton designed an Art Deco storefront of black carrara glass for 111 Church St (dated 1933 in Fig. 4 caption).
timeline.quote: subsequent sale in July 1933 to Hyman Abraham would make it possible.

timeline.what: A. Schulte cigar store at 115 Church St
timeline.detail: A New York regional chain moved in shortly after Abraham's 1933 purchase and stayed over twenty years.
timeline.quote: It would remain here for over twenty years, when in 1954 it closed and re-opened under local ownership as “Schulte’s of Vermont”.

timeline.detail: Abraham doubled his store into the 174 College space; Newton encased that part in cream-and-brown enameled sheet metal with glass-block windows and an 'ABRAHAM'S' parapet. Year from Fig. 4 caption.
timeline.quote: Here we see Hyman Abraham's 1946 alterations of the building, creating a disinctive double facade.

timeline.detail: Locally owned successor to A. Schulte; its owners declared bankruptcy and closed in 1958.
timeline.quote: even after Schulte’s of Vermont owners declared bankruptcy and closed shop in 1958.

timeline.what: Abraham buys final section; whole building sheathed
timeline.detail: Abraham bought the corner section in July 1955 and extended the modern facade over the entire exterior.
timeline.quote: was able to purchase this section of the building in July 1955.

timeline.what: A&W on the corner; Abraham's Camera Center begins
timeline.detail: In the 1960s A&W replaced the long-running tobacco and drug store on the corner, and Irwin Abrams started Abraham's Camera Center above the drug store.
timeline.quote: The 1960s finally put an end to the long-running tobacco and drug store on the corner when A&W, a long-running root beer and burger chain, moved into this location.

timeline.what: Irwin Abrams takes over after Hyman Abraham's death
timeline.detail: Abrams phased out the pharmacy by the 1980s and focused on photography.
timeline.quote: After Hyman’s death in 1974, Irwin Abrams would take over ownership of the business and phase out the pharmacy by the 80s, dedicating the business full time to photography.

timeline.detail: Leunig's opened in 1980 and gradually expanded through the building, adding a College St porch in the 1990s and a second-floor lounge.
timeline.quote: They first opened in 1980 and have been there since

timeline.detail: Abrams' son and an associate set up an advertising photography business in the building.
timeline.quote: His son and an associate even set up a professional advertising photography business in the building in 1982.

timeline.detail: Abraham's closed on Christmas Eve 2003, after 115 years overall.
timeline.quote: who finally closed on Christmas Eve 2003, after Irwin’s 45 years in the camera business here and Abraham’s 115 years overall.

timeline.detail: Leunig's got approval to replace the 'Abraham's' parapet letters; vinyl panels cover the older lettering.
timeline.quote: in 2006 they got approval to change the letters reading “Abraham’s” along the building’s parapet to read “Leunig’s”

timeline.detail: Leunig's Bistro & Cafe at 115 Church St and Danforth Pewter at 111 Church St.
timeline.quote: Today Leunig’s Bistro & Café is located at 115 Church Street and Danforth Pewter further north at 111 Church Street.

timeline.detail: The National Register nomination calls it possibly the oldest intact historic structure on Church Street.
timeline.quote: what “may be the oldest intact historic structure on Church Street” is attested to as early as 1825.

timeline.detail: A rear shed existed by the 1860s and was added onto in the late 1880s, per the 1889 Sanborn map; these clapboarded structures survive.
timeline.quote: As early as the 1860s there was a wooden shed in the rear, which was added onto in the late 1880s, as evidenced by 1889 Sanborn Map

timeline.detail: Adams, also an optician, occupied the store by 1881; it remained a jewelry store for many years.
timeline.quote: As early as 1881 the store was occupied by H.E. Adams, a watchmaker and jeweler

timeline.detail: Nelson Bero moved here from 99 Church St in 1910 and remodeled the store. The firm traced its history to Brinsmaid and Hildreth, founded 1793.
timeline.quote: Nelson Bero would continue on their business under The Bero Company after 1903 before moving a few doors down in 1910.

timeline.detail: Bero's sidewalk clock, called the 'unofficial timepiece of Burlington,' still stands.
timeline.quote: which was installed in 1925 and called the “unofficial timepiece of Burlington,”

timeline.what: Jim Detore photography and gift shop
timeline.detail: Detore bought the building after Bero closed and kept the clock; he died in January 1969.
timeline.quote: Bero operated at this location until 1967

timeline.detail: Moved in after Detore, then owned by Herbert Davis, who repaired the clock. Still there as of 2018 and the longest running business on the block.
timeline.quote: The Optical Center still occupies this location today and currently holds the distinction as the longest running business on this block of Church Street.

photos.caption: Facade of 107 Church Street, September 2018
photos.credit: Photograph by the author, taken September 30th, 2018

photos.caption: 107 Church Street in the last years of Bero's jewelry, with clock

timeline.detail: A plaque calls it possibly built in the 1820s; a structure appears here on the 1830 Ammi B. Young map.
timeline.quote: “one of the oldest surviving building on Church Street, possibly built in the 1820s”

timeline.detail: Per the plaque, the jewelry firm (page spells it 'Pangorn') formed here; J.E. Brinsmaid still operated here in the 1880s.
timeline.quote: the famous Pangorn and Brinsmaid jewelry store was formed here in 1832

timeline.what: 105: jewelry, Chinese laundry, Citizen's Coal Company
timeline.detail: 105 housed a jewelry store in the 1870s, a Chinese laundry in the 1880s and 1890s, then Citizen's Coal Company for over fifty years until 1955.
timeline.quote: then the headquarters for Citizen’s Coal Company for over fifty years, up until 1955.

timeline.detail: Start of a long line of restaurants at 103.
timeline.quote: opened in 1908 as Boston Lunch, renamed Queen City Café in 1925, then Liberty Restaurant in 1930

timeline.what: Fire starts in Boston Lunch kitchen
timeline.detail: The September 21, 1925 fire spread to adjacent wooden buildings; the fire marshal called them fire traps, but they were rebuilt.
timeline.quote: The first changing of hands was perhaps spurred on by a fire originating in the Boston Lunch kitchen on September 21st, 1925.
renamed Queen City Café in 1925

timeline.detail: Ran nearly sixty years; a remodeled Liberty reopened per a 1959 ad.
timeline.quote: then Liberty Restaurant in 1930

timeline.detail: Warehouses behind the building were demolished in the late 1950s for a parking lot.
timeline.quote: These were demolished in the late 1950s to make space for a parking lot

timeline.what: Two Guys restaurant; single restaurant fills building
timeline.detail: The Liberty was sold to two men who opened 'Two Guys'; one restaurant has filled the building since the late 1960s.
timeline.quote: The building, while housing a single restaurant since the late 1960s, has typically been two storefronts.

timeline.detail: The Office in the 1970s, Queen City Tavern in the 1980s and early 1990s. Facade modernized in the early 1980s.
timeline.quote: The Office in the 1970s, Queen City Tavern in the 1980s and early 1990s and Church Street Tavern since 1995.

timeline.detail: Church Street Tavern since 1995, single tenant as of 2018.
timeline.quote: Church Street Tavern since 1995.

photos.caption: 103-105 Church Street, Church Street Tavern, October 2018
photos.credit: Photograph by the author, taken September 30th, 2018

photos.caption: Plaque at 103 Church Street and parged false quoins
photos.credit: Photograph by the author, taken September 18th, 2018

photos.caption: 1882 business directory clipping showing jewelers at 99, 103 and 107

timeline.detail: Established in the 1880s; used the rear brick storehouse as a bakery; relocated 1912.
timeline.quote: In 101, as early as the 1880s, the Kent Brothers established their confectionary and grocery store which operated until relocation in 1912.

timeline.detail: Brinsmaid & Hildreth opened here in the early 1880s with a suspended street clock; Nelson Bero continued the business after 1903 and moved a few doors down in 1910.
timeline.quote: 99 Church Street has also been to home to long established businesses, starting with the first location in the early 1880s of Brinsmaid & Hildreth

timeline.detail: Opened the year after the Kents left; a bakery still operated here.
timeline.quote: The following year the Burlington Shoe Shine Parlors opened up on street level
In 1924, a candy store named Candyland moved in

timeline.detail: Operated under one name or another until the mid-1980s; candy stores since.
timeline.quote: only to be ousted by another shoe related business, Burlington Shoe Repairing Company in 1931

timeline.detail: The late-19th-century clapboarded Italianate building has been stuccoed since at least the early 1930s.
timeline.quote: however it has been stuccoed since at least the early 1930s

timeline.what: 99: Boston Fruit and Meat Market; Collegiate Shoppe
timeline.detail: A grocery for over twenty years, then several Depression-era businesses, including the Collegiate Shoppe joined to 97.
timeline.quote: A grocery store, Boston Fruit and Meat Market, was located there for over twenty years before several businesses came and went during the Great Depression.

timeline.detail: Operated until the 1970s.
timeline.quote: another shoe repair, The Shufix, came into the location in 1941 which operated there until the 1970s.

timeline.detail: October 22, 1943 fire started at Burlington Shoe Repair; the building lost its top floor of residences and was reduced to two stories.
timeline.quote: This building’s third-floor residences, however, were swiftly erased on October 22nd, 1943

timeline.what: Later tenants; Sweet Thing and The Sox Market (as of 2018)
timeline.detail: 99 housed an art supply in the 1980s and a t-shirt shop in the 1990s. As of 2018: Sweet Thing candy at 101, The Sox Market at 99.
timeline.quote: It currently houses two businesses, Sweet Thing, a candy store, at 101 Church Street and The Sox Market at 99 Church Street.

photos.credit: Photograph by the author, taken September 18th, 2018

timeline.detail: Building appears on the 1830 map; marked as Miss Kennedy's business on the 1862 map; advertised through the 1880s.
timeline.quote: it’s indicated as the business of Miss Kennedy on the 1862 Burlington Map.
jeweler-watchmaker-optician A.D. Bristol occupied the space until 1902

timeline.detail: Sometime in the 1890s the outside stair to the second floor was enclosed, connecting to 99-101.
timeline.quote: Sometime in the 1890s the exterior staircase accessing the second floor was closed in, connecting it to 99-101 Church; today this access to the second-story apartment is 97½.

timeline.what: Oriental rug store; R.W. Parish, Jeweler-Optician
timeline.detail: Demetrius Nour briefly ran a rug store, then R.W. Parish until the late 1920s.
timeline.quote: before it reverted to the block’s familiar formula under R.W. Parish, Jeweler-Optician, until the late 20s.

timeline.detail: Several clothing store incarnations in the 1930s and early 1940s.
timeline.quote: The location was then converted to a clothing store and had several incarnations during the 30s and early 40s.

timeline.detail: Temporary headquarters between clothing stores; the Democratic Party city headquarters followed two years later.
timeline.quote: this location was the temporary headquarters for a Republican mayoral candidate in 1941

timeline.detail: Stayed eleven years before moving to Florida; a children's clothing store followed.
timeline.quote: before another jeweler Ralph Van Gelder moved in later in 1943.

timeline.detail: Between the late 1950s and late 1960s two upper windows were replaced by one bay window.
timeline.quote: Sometime between the late 1950s and late 1960s, the two second floor windows were replaced with one large central bay window

timeline.detail: Fremeau's sought temporary space after a fire in its building further north on Church St.
timeline.quote: who was seeking temporary tenancy in 1974 after a fire in their building further north on Church Street

timeline.detail: Followed clothing stores that ran until 1986.
timeline.quote: would house more clothing establishments until 1986, when - yet again - a Republican campaign temporarily had an office here

timeline.detail: Cornell bought the property in 1993, made it her flagship and converted upstairs to an apartment; Kit Cornell followed after she moved.
timeline.quote: Local entrepreneur and clothing designer April Cornell would purchase the property in 1993

timeline.detail: Moved in 2007 and still there as of 2018.
timeline.quote: Garcia’s Tobacco Store would move in 2007

photos.credit: Photograph by the author, taken September 18th, 2018

timeline.what: Sion E. Howard dry goods store (predecessor)
timeline.detail: A small two-story building roughly where 93 Church now stands held Sion E. Howard's dry goods store, said to be the town's first cash store.
timeline.quote: Sion E. Howard, older brother of John Purple Howard, had a dry goods store as early as 1830

timeline.what: Built for Burritt Brothers drug store
timeline.detail: Four-story Italianate building built within a year of the Howard Opera House by the same architect; Burritt Bros. ran a drug store from construction through the 1880s. Stylized 'B' lintels survive.
timeline.quote: It was originally built for the Burritt Brothers, who operated a drug store out of it from its construction through the 1880s.

timeline.detail: After George LaFountain's 'Opera House Pharmacy,' Churchill took over and operated until the 1920s.
timeline.quote: who would take over in the 1896 and would operate there continuously until the 1920s.

timeline.detail: A firm including Hyman Abraham bought Churchill's store, dropped drugs and tobacco, and ran a luncheonette with a rear kitchen addition.
timeline.quote: In 1927, a newly incorporated firm Soda Luncheonettes, Inc., formed by three local businessmen including Hyman Abraham

timeline.detail: Building sold to David Stollman of Plattsburgh; remodeled with a 15-foot-deep plate glass and aluminum storefront. Operated fifteen years.
timeline.quote: The luncheonette would continue until 1938, when the whole building, which was indeed still owned by druggist George Churchill, was sold to David Stollman of Plattsburgh, NY

timeline.detail: Replaced Stollman's; owned by David Stollman and his son.
timeline.quote: Bernsol’s would endure until 1972

timeline.detail: During Stollman's tenancy the bank bought the building and installed a walk-up teller.
timeline.quote: During Stollman’s tenancy, Burlington Savings Bank would purchase the building and install a walk-up teller at the storefront.

timeline.detail: In the 1970s and 1980s.
timeline.quote: In the 1970s and 80s Magram’s would house their department store’s Children’s Shop in this location

timeline.detail: Nord Brue and Michael Dressell bought the buildings in 1989 for their hometown bagel shop; it closed December 2017.
timeline.quote: This downtown Bruegger’s would operate until its closing in December 2017.

timeline.what: Vacant; Burlington Bagel Bakery slated (as of 2018)
timeline.detail: Presently vacant; slated for Burlington Bagel Bakery, founded 1979.
timeline.quote: The location is slated to be occupied by Burlington Bagel Bakery

photos.credit: Photograph by the author, taken September 18th, 2018

photos.caption: Window lintel with letter 'B'
photos.credit: Photograph by the author, taken September 18th, 2018

timeline.detail: The bank likely occupied the corner from the 1820s until it moved in 1867. In 1869 the old building held a tailor's shop and a dwelling.
timeline.quote: This bank likely occupied this site from 1820s before its relocation in 1867

timeline.what: John P. Howard owns the lot
timeline.detail: The 1869 map shows John Purple Howard as owner; Sion Howard had died in 1866.
timeline.quote: the 1869 Burlington map makes clear that by this time his younger brother John P. Howard is the owner of this plot.

timeline.detail: Funded by John Purple Howard at $100,000 and designed by Stephen Decatur Hatch; stores on Church St with a theater above. Construction began November 1877 and finished February 1879.
timeline.quote: Construction began in November 1877

timeline.detail: Seated 1300 to 1400; red hipped roof.
timeline.quote: Construction was completed in February of 1879

timeline.detail: Howard built a three-story brick Italianate building just west with two Bank St stores.
timeline.quote: built another commercial building just west of the Opera House in 1880.

timeline.what: Willed to the Home for Destitute Children
timeline.detail: After Howard's death (1885) the building went to the Home, predecessor of Howard Center.
timeline.quote: John P. Howard willed the entire structure to the Home of Destitute Children.

timeline.detail: Rising fire insurance rates forced the theater to close.
timeline.quote: the Opera House was forced to stage its last performance on November 30th, 1904.

timeline.detail: Fig. 23 caption dates the removal to 1904; the text says it came shortly after the 1905 interior conversion.
timeline.quote: An aerial view from the top of Church Street showing the Howard Opera House's pyramidal roof that was removed in 1904.

timeline.detail: By spring 1905 the theater was being divided; W.G. Reynolds, the Old Bee Hive, E.E. Clarkson and the Blue Store expanded and stayed for decades.
timeline.quote: by the spring interior girders were in place and sleepers being laid to divide up the former theatre into more useful space.

timeline.detail: Sometime between 1912 and 1919 the gap to the Bank St building was filled.
timeline.quote: Sometime between 1912 and 1919, the small amount of space separating this block from the Opera House was finally infilled

timeline.what: The Fashion Shop moves to corner (later Magram's)
timeline.detail: Barney Magram became partner in The Fashion Shop (founded 1914) and moved it from 52 Church to the corner.
timeline.quote: In 1943, Barney Magram would become a partner in The Fashion Shop, founded in 1914 by Max Glass, and move it from 52 Church to W.G. Reynold’s vacated corner sport.

timeline.detail: Barney became sole owner and added his surname.
timeline.quote: After rising to sole owner in 1952, Barney would add his surname to the business

timeline.detail: After Barney died in 1969, Murray Daitchman expanded the store and added a travertine marble arcade around the ground floor.
timeline.quote: Barney passed in 1969, after which his son-in-law and successor Murray Daitchman expanded the store to 55,000 square feet within the old Opera House.

timeline.detail: Magram's sold to Nord Brue and Michael Dressell and shrank to two floors.
timeline.quote: to sell it off in 1989 to two local businessmen, Nord Brue and Michael Dressell, founders of Breugger’s Bagels.

timeline.detail: Magram's closed January 1991; a 9-month renovation replaced the arcade with separate historic-style storefronts.
timeline.quote: it’s ultimate closing in January 1991 opened the door for the new owners to rethink the space

timeline.detail: Tenants: Slate, Ten Thousand Villages, Frog Hollow Craft Center, Pascolo Ristorante, ECCO Clothing; Simon Pearce at 157 Bank.
timeline.quote: Current tenants include, south to north on Church, Slate, Ten Thousand Villages, Frog Hollow Craft Center, Pascolo Ristorante and ECCO Clothing

pages.source_label: UVM HP206, The City Hall Block - College Street to Main Street, West Side, by Adam King, 2018

places.address: Corner of Church and College (King Tavern, Strong Block, YMCA Block site)

timeline.detail: Several sources place the jail on the corner from 1797 to 1803; Levi Allen reportedly died there.
timeline.quote: Burlington's jail occupied that corner during a brief period from 1797-1803

timeline.detail: Gideon King's son reportedly owned a tavern on the corner as early as 1798, later expanded to roughly today's footprint.
timeline.quote: Lyman King, Gideon King's son and sheriff of the county, is said to have owned a tavern on that corner as early as 1798

timeline.detail: Thomas ran it as the Burlington Hotel until selling to W.L. Strong in 1829.
timeline.quote: who ran it as the Burlington Hotel until selling it to hardware store proprietor W.L. Strong in 1829.

timeline.detail: Strong divided the wooden building into Church St storefronts.
timeline.quote: Strong was also responsible for dividing the building into the smaller Church Street storefronts and letting them to tenants.

timeline.what: Samuel Huntington print shop, stationery and bindery
timeline.detail: Strong sold Huntington a 40 by 50 foot corner in 1837. The building inscription dates his tenure 1837 to 1888; elsewhere the page says his business dates from 1839.
timeline.quote: Samuel Huntington, who operated a print shop, stationery, and book bindery beginning in 1837

timeline.detail: The page says Strong sold to the YMCA the year before the 1887 fire, but also cites a plot sold in 1876.
timeline.quote: Just the previous year to the fire, Strong had sold his interest in the block to the YMCA

timeline.detail: Fire began in a basement storeroom and destroyed the building.
timeline.quote: Mercantile activity came to an abrupt hiatus on that block in 1887 however, when much of the block was destroyed by fire.

timeline.detail: Romanesque stone and brick building by Fuller and Wheeler of Albany, shared by the YMCA and Huntington's business.
timeline.quote: The 1889 edition of the Sanborn map shows the new structure under construction, subsequently known as the YMCA Block, which had broken ground the previous year.

timeline.detail: Successor to Huntington's business occupied the Huntington section.
timeline.quote: the Huntington part of the building would ultimately be occupied by the McAuliffe Paper Company beginning in 1912

timeline.detail: Fire found after 4 a.m. on February 1, 1928; loss estimated at $500,000 to $750,000.
timeline.quote: being destroyed by fire in 1928.

The Burlington YMCA building as built, postcard
YMCA building's east wall collapsing

timeline.detail: Rebuilt after the 1928 fire on the former Huntington section; reuses the YMCA Block's red sandstone ground floor. Three-story brick office building built by James Cashman.
timeline.quote: was rebuilt by the MacAuliffe Paper Company to become known as what is now 117 Church Street.

timeline.detail: Carved names and dates mark Huntington (1837 to 1888) and McAuliffe (1912 to the 1928 fire). Stained glass advertising books and stationery survives, obscured by awnings.
timeline.quote: 1837 to 1888 are the dates during which Samuel Huntington's businesses occupied that corner prior to the construction of the YMCA Block

photos.caption: Extant corner of the former YMCA block today

timeline.detail: Neoclassical bank by Harper and West, built by Cashman on the YMCA section; wraps around the McAuliffe Building. A financial and office building since 1931, with retail storefronts as of 2018.
timeline.quote: Since its construction in 1931, the building has been a financial institution and office building, and today includes retail storefronts.

places.address: Ethan Allen Engine Co. No. 4 firehouse (no street number given)

timeline.what: Ethan Allen Engine Co. No. 4 firehouse and club
timeline.detail: City raised $15,000 for a Romanesque brick firehouse with an 85-foot hose tower and clubrooms, designed by the A.B. Fisher firm. Served until the Central Fire Station opened.
timeline.quote: In 1889 the city (whose leaders were often members of the Ethan Allen Club) raised $15,000 for construction of a dedicated firehouse just south of the YMCA Block.

timeline.detail: Occupied the building after the fire company left until 1967; the city then scheduled demolition.
timeline.quote: following the move, the building was occupied by the Burlington Police Department until 1967.

timeline.detail: New York Times critic Ada Louise Huxtable praised the building; national attention helped win a $63,000 HUD grant.
timeline.quote: In her article of September 14, 1969, entitled 'the Bucolic Bulldozer,"

timeline.detail: Saved from demolition and listed.
timeline.quote: ultimately aided its being listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1970.

timeline.detail: Renovated; UVM continuing education occupied it.
timeline.quote: Starting in 1974, the former firehouse was occupied by UVM's continuing education department as the Church Street Center.

timeline.detail: Offices, galleries and studios since the mid-1990s.
timeline.quote: Since the mid-1990s the firehouse has been occupied by Burlington City Arts

places.address: City Hall (Court House Square east side; no street number given)

timeline.detail: Built in the center of Court House Square. The page elsewhere dates the center-square court houses 1797 to 1829.
timeline.quote: the original Court House was constructed directly in the center of Court House Square in 1795.

timeline.detail: Wooden building with a steeple; burned in June 1829, blamed on a lantern.
timeline.quote: The first Court House was relatively short-lived, being supplanted by a new building in 1802, and this replacement served the town until 1829.

timeline.what: New Court House on east side of square
timeline.detail: Federal-style building with an oversized octagonal lantern; town offices below.
timeline.quote: its replacement was constructed in the middle of the east side of the square in 1830.

timeline.detail: Palladian brick building designed by T.S. Whitby, south of the Court House; first town meeting held there 1854. Poor acoustics.
timeline.quote: The so-called Town-City Hall, indicative of this transitional phase in Burlington's history, was first constructed on the site in 1853

timeline.what: Fletcher Free Library in old Court House
timeline.detail: Mary L. and Mary M. Fletcher gave $10,000 each; city approved conversion November 3, 1873. Library stayed nearly thirty years.
timeline.quote: Mary L. and Mary M. Fletcher, two local citizens of means, decided in 1873 to donate $10,000 each

timeline.detail: Old Court House left essentially vacant.
timeline.quote: a fourth in Vermont was applied for by the Fletcher Free Library and built in Burlington in 1901.

timeline.detail: GAR Stannard post took the upper floor; city departments below.
timeline.quote: it was essentially vacant until 1905, when city aldermen moved to allow the Stannard post of the Grand Army of The Republic to occupy the upper, main floor of the building

timeline.what: Earthquake closes old City Hall to gatherings
timeline.detail: February 28, 1925 quake; the crumbling hall was closed to large meetings, spurring replacement.
timeline.quote: On Saturday the 28 th of February, 1925

timeline.detail: McKim, Mead and White design, built by James Cashman for $475,000; essentially unaltered.
timeline.quote: After its construction was completed in 1928 at a cost of $475,000

timeline.what: Building on corner since at least 1830
timeline.detail: A three-story side-gabled masonry building stood here for decades with a clothing store on the first floor.
timeline.quote: it is no surprise that a building has occupied the site since at least 1830.

timeline.what: Clothing stores and upstairs photography studio
timeline.detail: Clothing stores under various proprietors until the 1910s, including Stiles & Kelley; a photography studio ran until 1925 and a dentist rented space.
timeline.quote: These photographs and directories document the presence of a clothing store at this address operated by different proprietors until the 1910s.

timeline.what: Paul D. Kelley grocery; building demolished
timeline.detail: Kelley's grocery briefly used the first floor before demolition in 1925.
timeline.quote: Prior to its demolition in 1925, the first floor operated briefly as Paul D. Kelley’s grocery store.

timeline.detail: Colonial Revival bank by James W. O'Connor, commissioned 1925, with Vermont marble, brick and slate. Plaque reads 'Burlington Trust Co. 1882-1826' (sic).
timeline.quote: this building was replaced with a beautiful, high-style Colonial Revival structure in 1926

timeline.detail: The trust merged with Howard National Bank in 1952 and sold the building.
timeline.quote: In that year, the building was sold to Miles & Riley, proprietors of a men’s clothing store that operated until 1969

timeline.detail: Novelty woodworking retail outlet.
timeline.quote: when the Kennedy Brothers Company purchased the property to use as a retail outlet for their novelty wood-working business

timeline.detail: Tony Perry bought it in 1981; Lawrence Atkin redesigned the interior and Wendy Coop painted a history mural. Still there as of 2018.
timeline.quote: this iconic property was purchased by Tony Perry in 1981, who opened the Sweetwaters Restaurant that still occupies the site.

timeline.detail: First structure on the lot: a small one-story building.
timeline.quote: The 1885 Sanborn map was the first one to show a small, almost square, one-story, composition-roofed building there, occupied by a news dealer.

timeline.detail: Footprint doubled in the 1890s; two stories by 1900.
timeline.quote: The building was enlarged in the 1890s, doubling the footprint, and by 1900 it was two stories tall
From around 1894 to 1912, #124 was a florist shop operated by John Wilson.

timeline.detail: Back to one story by 1912; part of #126 by 1919.
timeline.quote: by 1919, the property had been absorbed by its southern neighbor, #126.

timeline.detail: Wood-framed building divided into barber shop, market and eating saloon.
timeline.quote: According to the 1869 Sanborn map, there was a one-and-a-half-story, wood-framed commercial building covering these two properties.

timeline.detail: Own one-story building; a second story was added five years later. M.S. Storrs sold meat and poultry in the 1880s.
timeline.quote: By 1885, #126 had its own independent structure, a one-story, composition-roofed meat market.

timeline.what: F. Howes & Co.; tailor and fruit shop
timeline.detail: F. Howes briefly occupied it around 1900; later split into 126 and 126A.
timeline.quote: F. Howes & Co. briefly occupied the building around 1900

timeline.detail: Properties merged again.
timeline.quote: By 1912, the properties had merged again and accommodated a barbershop.

timeline.detail: One-story restaurant enveloping #124 until the Burlington Trust building took over the site.
timeline.quote: #126 enveloped #124, comprising a one-story, wood-framed, composition-roofed restaurant, Burlington Lunch.

timeline.what: Buildings on site since at least 1830
timeline.detail: Larger block shown on 1853 and 1857 maps.
timeline.quote: Buildings of various size have stood at this site since at least 1830.

timeline.detail: Present two-story frame building may date to the late 19th century.
timeline.quote: the 1885 Sanborn map shows a bisected structure matching that of today, which housed a news and confectionary shop at #128 and a tobacconist at #130.

timeline.detail: Star Restaurant soon moved to #144.
timeline.quote: By 1894, #128 was a barbershop and #130 was the Star Restaurant

timeline.detail: Until the late 1910s.
timeline.quote: in 1900, the barbershop had become Paul D. Kelley’s grocery store, which remained there until the late 1910s

timeline.detail: Run by H. E. Cutler, then Hollis W. Clark, from about 1905. Facades brick-faced by 1919.
timeline.quote: #130 was a photography studio from about 1905 to 1940, operated first by H. E. Cutler and later by Hollis W. Clark.

timeline.what: Gover's Radio Shop, Tanner's Barber Shop, Pure Food Bakery
timeline.detail: Subdivided in the early 1940s.
timeline.quote: when it was subdivided to accommodate two storefronts, Gover’s Radio Shop at #128 and Tanner’s Barber Shop at #130.

timeline.detail: Rebuilt circa 1965; one of few Carrara glass facades left on Church St.
timeline.quote: The façade was rebuilt again circa 1965 in its present Moderne-style form

timeline.detail: Northern shop now numbered #126 (Global Pathways since 1996); southern now #128 (Maven); design firm upstairs.
timeline.quote: The northern shop, now numbered #126, has housed Global Pathways, a jewelry and mineral store, since 1996

timeline.detail: Before Mechanics Lane bisected the block.
timeline.quote: This lot on Church Street has been occupied by a structure since 1830

timeline.detail: In the 1860s a glazier and grocer below with a barbershop above; a rear wooden building at 12 Skinner's Lane.
timeline.quote: more insight is available regarding the structure that stood there from at least 1853 to 1900.

timeline.detail: Meat market from the late 1880s through 1960, run by F. Howes & Co. after the 1901 rebuild.
timeline.quote: the first floor of #132-134 remained a meat market from the late 1880s through 1960
This reconstruction was necessitated by a fire in 1900 that destroyed the building.

timeline.detail: Three-story masonry block with granite 'HYLAND' tablet. Upper floors later used by Company M, Vermont National Guard, Knights of Pythias, a suspender factory and the Burlington Production Credit Association.
timeline.quote: In spite of its total reconstruction in 1901

timeline.detail: Fire destroyed the third floor; west facade rebuilt with arched openings. Alterations keep it from being a contributing building in the historic district.
timeline.quote: Fire struck the building sometime in the 1960s, destroying the third floor

timeline.detail: Bar occupying the ground floor.
timeline.quote: which open into Ake’s Place, the bar that currently occupies it.

timeline.detail: A large square building stood at the corner of Skinners Lane by the 1850s.
timeline.quote: In 1830, this property was occupied by two narrow structures fronting Church Street

timeline.detail: In the 1860s a two-story wood-framed building with three storefronts.
timeline.quote: It housed, from north to south, a saddler, an eating saloon, and an upholsterer.

timeline.detail: The page says the 1860s building was replaced by a similar one in the 1870s, though it also suggests the 1860s structure remains.
timeline.quote: This structure was replaced by a similar one in the 1870s.

timeline.detail: Run by W. B. Craven above its restaurant from the 1880s through the 1900s.
timeline.quote: The Hotel Champlain, operated by W. B. Craven, occupied the upper stories of these addresses above its restaurant from the 1880s through the 1900s.

timeline.what: #136: fish dealer, then F. Howes & Co.
timeline.detail: Fish and oyster dealer in the 1880s; F. Howes meat market in the 1890s until moving to #134 in 1901.
timeline.quote: then F. Howes & Co.’s meat market throughout the 1890s, until they moved across Mechanics Lane to #134 in 1901.

timeline.detail: Operated through the 1960s.
timeline.quote: By 1900, the roof had been redone in metal and #136 was occupied by Bessey’s News Co., which operated there through the 1960s.

timeline.detail: #136 1/2 split off from #136 by 1926.
timeline.quote: #136½ was shaved off of #136 by 1926, when it was a shoe shine parlor.

timeline.detail: In the 1920s the west facade was extended upward and stuccoed.
timeline.quote: In the 1920s, the west façade was extended upward to its present form

timeline.detail: Edythe Bushnell ran the ladies' clothing shop until 1953; the Kenyons ran it through the 1970s.
timeline.quote: Edythe A. Bushnell founded the Bushnell Shop there in 1935 and operated it until her retirement in 1953

timeline.what: Freeman, French, Freeman and Vermont YWCA (#138)
timeline.detail: Rented space in the 1930s and 1940s.
timeline.quote: The architecture firm of Freeman, French, Freeman and the Vermont YWCA both rented space at #138 in the 1930s and 40s.

timeline.what: Red Square, Half Lounge, tattoo parlor, Red Onion Cafe (as of 2018)
timeline.detail: #140 was a barbershop for much of the 20th century (Eldon H. Dickson, then Ancel R. Godette).
timeline.quote: It is currently home to the Red Onion Café.

timeline.detail: Then housed Enos Peterson's store; a building of the same footprint stood here since at least 1830.
timeline.quote: Hiram H. Reynolds commissioned this loadbearing brick building after purchasing the property in 1864

timeline.what: Reynolds' restaurant in new Italianate building
timeline.detail: Three-story brick building opened December 1866 at a cost of $10,000; bracketed cornice added by 1885.
timeline.quote: The three-story Italianate building at 142-144 Church Street was constructed in 1866
Reynolds operated his dining saloon until 1895, when W. C. Hoag bought it and changed the name to the Star Restaurant

timeline.detail: Asian restaurant under successive owners since 1921.
timeline.quote: It has operated as an Asian restaurant since 1921 under a succession of different owners.

timeline.detail: Through the late 1970s.
timeline.quote: which became the Lotus Restaurant from 1947 through the late 1970s.
In 2016, Gaku Ramen became the latest in the legacy of such restaurants at this site.

timeline.what: Oldest building on this part of the block
timeline.detail: Dates to at least the early 1850s (Presdee & Edwards map). The page says the site looks vacant on 'Ammi Burnham Young's 1833 map'.
timeline.quote: The building located at 146-148 Church Street is the oldest one on this part of the block, dating to at least the early 1850s

timeline.detail: Furniture warehouse in the 1860s; Jones & Isham flour, feed, grain and hay from the 1880s until the 1910s. Barbers here almost continuously since the 1880s.
timeline.quote: by the 1880s had become Jones & Isham’s flour, feed, grain, and hay store, which they operated until the 1910s.

timeline.detail: Restaurant since the 1920s, including Burlington Lunch and Hi-Hat Restaurant. Storefront covered in black Carrara glass mid-century.
timeline.quote: #148 has housed a restaurant since the 1920s, including Burlington Lunch and Hi-Hat Restaurant.

timeline.detail: Lost cornice and attic opening; Church St wall parged with stucco afterward.
timeline.quote: a small arched opening at the attic level until a fire in February 1970
Below, the storefront was covered with a rough-cut, random-coursed stone veneer in 2008.

timeline.what: Building on corner since at least 1830
timeline.detail: Enlarged or replaced by 1853; shown as three-story gabled building in 1857 Walling vignette.
timeline.quote: The northeast corner of this intersection has been occupied by a building since at least 1830.

timeline.detail: Combined with its Main St neighbor; Church St stores with eating saloon, harness store, barber; hotel opened December 1868 under Rollin Pease and Orvis S. Storrs.
timeline.quote: This structure was enlarged or rebuilt and combined with its Main Street neighbor in 1868 to form the Allen House

timeline.detail: Dry goods and shoes; liquor fines and nuisance complaints followed.
timeline.quote: By 1871, #152 housed Lyman & Allen’s, a specialty dry goods store, and Drew & Davis sold shoes at #154.

timeline.detail: Portions demolished for the Vermont Life Insurance building and the Exchange Block.
timeline.quote: by 1877, the Allen House was in decline.

timeline.what: Exchange Block opens; E. P. Shaw clothing at #156
timeline.detail: Three-story Italianate brick block with iron and plate glass storefronts and galvanized iron cornice; #156 lit April 2, 1878. Clothing at #156 for about forty years, then a pharmacy, Burlington Sweet Shop and Upton's Sandwich Shoppe.
timeline.quote: who gathered on the evening of April 2, 1878 to see the storefront of #156 lit for the first time.
in the 1880s, W. B. McKillip & Co. sold all manner of “fancy groceries” at #154

timeline.detail: Long-term upstairs tenant.
timeline.quote: One long-term resident was Miss Mary E. McCarthy, a tailoress who rented a room at #152 from about 1900 to 1926.
the Burlington Fruit Co. operated out of #150 from around 1906-1926.

timeline.what: Enos A. Howard cigar store, then Howard's Grill (#154)
timeline.detail: Grill included billiards and bowling.
timeline.quote: By 1912, Enos A. Howard had acquired #154, in which he opened first a cigar store and then Howard’s Grill

timeline.detail: Rooftop nameplate lost.
timeline.quote: was unfortunately lost to a fire in 1962 that destroyed the third floor of #150-154.

timeline.detail: Eastern Mediterranean mezze restaurant.
timeline.quote: It is still a restaurant today - now home to Honey Road
